title: Moral Luck
rootClaim: Moral luck invalidates the core Kantian intuition that individuals should be morally judged only for factors within their conscious control.

branches.text: Control Principle Paradox: We intuitively hold that agents are only morally assessable for what is within their control, yet our actual moral judgments depend heavily on luck.

children.text: Resultant Moral Luck: Two equally negligent drivers commit identical reckless acts; one hits a pedestrian due to unexpected luck, while the other drives home safely. We judge the first far more harshly.
Epistemic vs Moral Blame Defense: Differences in punishment reflect pragmatic legal deterrence and evidentiary clarity rather than true differences in moral guilt.
Moral Resentment Asymmetry: The driver who strikes a child experiences genuine, appropriate 'agent-regret' that the safe driver logically cannot experience, proving moral luck is real.
Psychological vs Moral Blameworthiness: Agent-regret is an emotional byproduct of causal responsibility, not a reflection of moral blameworthiness.
Circumstantial Moral Luck: Ordinary citizens in 1930s Germany who became Nazi collaborators were exposed to unique historical circumstances that citizens in peacetime democracies never faced.
Constitutive Moral Luck: An individual's temperament, empathy levels, and biological impulse control are determined by genetics and upbringing outside their control.

branches.text: Kantian Moral Purity Defense: True moral worth attaches strictly to the good will and inner intention, regardless of external consequences or luck.

children.text: Deontological Imperative: If moral luck exists, morality becomes arbitrary, reducing moral praise and blame to an unfair lottery.
Incoherent Character Paradox: Denying moral luck forces us to judge people purely by abstract unseen intentions, ignoring all real-world actions, outcomes, and character manifestations.

definitions.description: A phenomenon where a significant aspect of a person's moral assessment depends on factors beyond their control.
The moral principle that people cannot be morally assessed for what is not their fault, or for what is due to factors beyond their control.
Luck in the way things turn out following an action or choice.
Luck in the surroundings, opportunities, and historical situation an agent finds themselves in.
Bernard Williams' concept of a specific form of regret an agent feels towards their own past actions when those actions cause bad outcomes, even without fault.
